newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr worn down as bears bet on job gloom.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr worn down as bears bet on job gloom.

text.p: The Australian dollar was 1/2 cent down and under pressure late Wednesday amid signs of renewed selling from U.S. hedge funds and Japanese investors.
Much of the move happened in slow motion as speculators ground away support in the hope of triggering stop-loss sales which would then snowball into a substantial slide.

The important US$0.7350 chart bulwark had held so far and dealers had been impressed by the depth of demand the last time it tested these levels a fortnight ago. But they suspected bears were betting a weak labour report, due Thursday, would rekindle rate cut talk and see the A$ test 18-month lows at US$0.7310.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) bears had chased it to US$0.7355/60 from an early US$0.7373/78 and US$0.7392/97 late here Tuesday.
They were also encouraged by a dismal technical outlook following the failure to sustain a short covering rally past 75 cents last week or even a modest rise to US$0.7420 overnight.
To many, the retreats confirmed the A$'s four month old downtrend from 80 cents had further to run and may yet reach the US$0.7250 target, if not the 1995 low of US$0.7070.
A rally back above US$0.7440 was needed to counter immediate pressure and it would take a break of both US$0.7505 and US$0.7550 resistance to reverse the trend.
But the chief motivator for sellers was uncertainty over monetary policy which, contrary to bulls' expectations, had not been put to rest by last week's official rate cut.

Most analysts did indeed think that was probably the last in the easing cycle, but few were willing to rule out another given indicators of economic activity were mixed at best and underlying inflation looked certain to stay near record lows for a few quarters yet.
The lacklustre nature of the economy was illustrated by the NAB July business survey which found conditions deteriorated in July, so losing all the modest gain made in June.
NAB found a small improvement in conditions for retailing, wholesaling, construction and transport, but these were more than offset by a deterioration in services and manufacturing.
Labour shedding also increased, with the employment index down at negative five from negative one in June.
This was alarming for dollar bulls since official labour data for July are due Thursday and any weakness was certain to kindle talk of another easing.
Analysts expect jobs growth to pick up to around 25,000 in July from 11,900 in June, but even added together that would not compensate for the shock 40,300 fall recorded in May.

Such a result would also leave unemployment stubbornly high at 8.6 percent and it should be remembered the Reserve Bank's charter commits it to maintaining full employment as well as controlling inflation.

Anything less than a 20,000 increase in employment would be considered soft and a fall -- which no analyst was looking for but none would rule out given the volatility of this series -- would see the money market begin to price in another rate cut.
Conversely, analysts cautioned a big monthly rise in jobs was statistically overdue and, with the market biased short, such an outcome would see the dollar rally sharply.

Elsewhere, the dollar held firm on the mark at 1.3817/34 from 1.3808/21 but was well short of a six-year offshore high around 1.3920 struck after the Bundesbank passed up a chance to fire a policy warning shot about the mark's weakness.
It also ran into profit taking on the yen after an official at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo said Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. was on a rising trend and may become a source of friction.
The dollar was at 87.67/77 yen from Tuesday's 87.62/72 and off an 88.22 high. In trade weighted terms it eased to 57.9 from a previous 58.1 finsih.
